weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test (suggested): Times — 1) 3:25 2) 7:50 3) 12:05 4) 9:15 (quarter past 9) 5) 4:30 (half past 4) 6) 10:45 (quarter to 11) 7) 6:10 8) 1:55 9) 8:35 10) 11:20. a.m./p.m.: breakfast a.m.; dinner p.m.; bedtime 8:00 at night p.m.; 10:00 in the morning a.m. Money: a) 3 dimes + 2 nickels = 40¢ b) $1 − 55¢ = 45¢ c) $10 + $5 + $1 = $16 d) 2 quarters + 3 pennies = 53¢ e) $20 − $8 = $12 f) 4 dimes + 1 quarter = 65¢. Proficient: 17/20.

weeks.prep: Measuring tape and a roll of adding-machine tape (or taped-together paper strips) and markers. Prepare 4 partly labeled number lines and 6 problems for Friday.
misconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of spaces (jumps). Each jump is the distance between marks; start at 0 with no jump counted yet.
Assuming every number line counts by 1. Look at two labeled marks and find the jump size first.

days.guide: Lay the measuring tape beside a number line: both start at 0 with equal spaces. On adding-machine tape, mark 0–100 with tick marks every 5 and label them.

questions.q: How is a number line like a ruler?
questions.a: Both start at 0 and have equal spaces between numbers.

questions.q: If marks go by 5s, what comes after 35?

days.guide: Show 35 as a length from 0 to 35. Then jump +20 to 55, and from 35 jump −12 to 23.

questions.q: Show 35 + 20.
questions.a: Start at 35, jump 20 to land on 55.

questions.q: Show 35 − 12.
questions.a: Start at 35, jump back 10 to 25, back 2 more to 23.

days.guide: Fill missing numbers on number lines counting by 2s, 5s, and 10s; find the jump size first.

questions.a: 16 (counting by 2s).

days.guide: Solve 8 problems on open number lines, labeling jumps.

questions.q: 48 + 25 on a number line.
90 − 34 on a number line.

days.guide: Give the quiz: label 4 number lines and solve 6 problems with jumps.

weeks.assessment_key: Number line quiz (suggested): label missing numbers — 1) 0, 5, __, 15, __ → 10, 20 2) 40, 50, __, 70 → 60 3) 12, 14, __, 18 → 16 4) 75, 80, __, 90 → 85. Problems on number lines: a) 35 + 20 = 55 b) 35 − 12 = 23 c) 48 + 25 = 73 d) 90 − 34 = 56 e) 27 + 46 = 73 f) 63 − 28 = 35. Proficient: 9/10 with jumps shown.

weeks.prep: Rulers, yardstick or tape, string, yarn, scissors. Choose a small rectangle (table or rug) for Tuesday. Prepare 8 length word problems for Friday.
misconceptions: Adding only two sides to find the distance around a rectangle. Walk a finger around all 4 sides and add all 4.
Mixing units in one problem. Underline the units and keep them the same.

days.guide: Read each length story, draw a bar or number line, and write an equation with units.

questions.q: A ribbon is 45 cm. 18 cm is cut off. How long is it now?
Ropes of 36 in and 25 in are tied end to end. Total length?
questions.a: 61 inches.

days.guide: Measure each side of a table or rug and add all 4 sides to find the distance around.

questions.q: A table is 40 in long and 25 in wide. What is the distance around?
How many sides do you add for a rectangle?
questions.a: 4 sides.

days.guide: Each family member does a standing long jump; measure from the start line to the back of the nearest heel. Write compare problems.

questions.q: Lia jumped 52 in and Max jumped 39 in. How much farther did Lia jump?
questions.a: 13 inches.

questions.q: Where do you measure a jump to?
questions.a: From the start line to the back of the heel closest to the line.

days.guide: Solve 4 two-step length problems with number lines.

questions.q: A string is 80 cm. Two 25 cm pieces are cut off. How much is left?
One board is 30 in. Another is 20 in longer. How long are both together?
questions.a: 80 in (the second is 50 in; 30 + 50).

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test: 8 length word problems with number lines and equations.

questions.q: A path is 50 m; you walked 32 m. How far is left?
A snake is 28 cm and grows 9 cm. How long now?
questions.a: 37 cm.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test (suggested 8): 1) Ribbon 45 cm, 18 cm cut off → 27 cm 2) Ropes 36 in + 25 in → 61 in 3) Lia jumped 52 in, Max 39 in → 13 in farther 4) Fence sides 20, 15, 20, 15 ft → 70 ft 5) String 80 cm, two 25 cm pieces cut → 30 cm left 6) Board 64 in, need 100 in → 36 in more 7) Snake 28 cm grows 9 cm → 37 cm 8) Path 50 m, walked 32 m → 18 m left. Each needs a number line or equation. Proficient: 7/8.

weeks.prep: Counters (20), a basket of socks or shoes, hundreds chart, crayons, linking cubes.
misconceptions: Deciding odd/even from the tens digit (thinking 32 is odd). Only the ones digit decides.
Thinking 0 is neither odd nor even. 0 has no leftover, so it is even.

days.guide: Pair up counters or socks for numbers 1–20. If every item has a partner, the number is even; one left over means odd. Record in a two-column chart.

questions.q: Is 9 odd or even? How do you know?
questions.a: Odd — 4 pairs and 1 left over.

questions.q: Is 12 odd or even?
questions.a: Even — 6 pairs, none left over.

days.guide: Write each even number to 20 as a double (12 = 6 + 6) and build it with two equal cube towers.

questions.q: Write 14 as two equal addends.
Write 18 as two equal addends.

days.guide: Color the even numbers on a hundreds chart and look at the ones digits (0, 2, 4, 6, 8). Predict 47 and 86.

questions.q: Is 47 odd or even?
questions.a: Odd — it ends in 7.

questions.q: Is 86 odd or even?
questions.a: Even — it ends in 6.

days.guide: Test even + even, odd + odd, and even + odd with 10 examples each. The child writes the rules.

questions.q: What is odd + odd?
What is even + odd?
questions.a: Odd (e.g., 4 + 3 = 7). Even + even is even.

days.guide: Give the quiz: classify 15 numbers or groups and write 5 even numbers as equal addends.

questions.q: Is 0 odd or even?
questions.a: Even.

questions.q: Write 20 as equal addends.

weeks.assessment_key: Odd/even quiz (suggested 15): 7 odd, 12 even, 15 odd, 20 even, 9 odd, 14 even, 47 odd, 86 even, 33 odd, 18 even, 101 odd, 56 even, a group of 11 counters odd, a group of 16 counters even, 0 even. Equal addends: 8 = 4 + 4; 10 = 5 + 5; 14 = 7 + 7; 18 = 9 + 9; 20 = 10 + 10. Proficient: 18/20.

weeks.prep: Counters, an egg carton, a muffin tin, grid paper. Prepare 8 array pictures and 4 equations for Friday.
misconceptions: Adding the number of rows and columns (a 3-by-4 array counted as 3 + 4 = 7). Count the objects: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Making rows of unequal length. In an array, every row has the same number.

days.guide: Make 4 groups of 3 counters. Write 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. Repeat with other equal groups.

questions.q: 4 groups of 3: repeated addition and total?
5 groups of 2?

days.guide: Find arrays at home (egg carton: 2 rows of 6; muffin tin: 3 rows of 4). Write repeated addition by rows and by columns.

questions.q: An egg carton has 2 rows of 6. Repeated addition?
A muffin tin has 3 rows of 4. Total?

days.guide: Build arrays up to 5 by 5 and draw them on grid paper. Write two equations for each (by rows and by columns).

questions.q: 3 rows with 5 in each row: two equations?
How many in 4 rows of 4?

days.guide: Solve 6 array stories with drawings and repeated addition.

questions.q: There are 4 rows of chairs with 5 chairs each. How many chairs?
3 rows of 3 cookies. How many cookies?

days.guide: Give the quiz: repeated addition for 8 arrays and draw arrays for 4 equations.

questions.q: Draw an array for 4 + 4.
questions.a: 2 rows of 4.

questions.q: 5 rows of 5?

weeks.assessment_key: Array quiz (suggested): 1) 2 rows of 5 → 5 + 5 = 10 2) 3 rows of 4 → 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 3) 4 rows of 3 → 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 4) 5 rows of 2 → 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10 5) 3 rows of 5 → 15 6) 4 rows of 4 → 16 7) 5 rows of 5 → 25 8) 2 rows of 3 → 6. Draw: a) 3 + 3 + 3 → 3 rows of 3 b) 4 + 4 → 2 rows of 4 c) 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 → 4 rows of 5 d) 2 + 2 + 2 → 3 rows of 2. Proficient: 11/12.

weeks.prep: Grid paper, square tiles or square crackers. Prepare the 12-item Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Thinking 2 rows of 6 and 6 rows of 2 have different totals. Turn the array to show it's the same 12.
Guessing odd/even from the row size (3 rows of 4 = 12 is even). Find the total, then check the ones digit.

days.guide: Build arrays with tiles or crackers and write 10 repeated-addition equations.

questions.q: 5 rows of 3 tiles: total?
2 rows of 4 crackers?

days.guide: Design a garden with 4 rows of 5 plants (20) and other arrays. Decide whether each total is odd or even.

questions.q: 4 rows of 5 plants: total, odd or even?
questions.a: 20, even.

questions.q: 3 rows of 3 plants?
questions.a: 9, odd.

days.guide: Find all rectangular arrays that make 12 using tiles.

questions.q: Find arrays that make 12.
questions.a: 1 row of 12, 2 rows of 6, 3 rows of 4 (and 4 of 3, 6 of 2, 12 of 1).

questions.q: Is 12 odd or even?
questions.a: Even.

days.guide: Solve 6 mixed problems on arrays, equal groups, and odd/even.

questions.q: 3 bags with 5 apples each. Total? Odd or even?
questions.a: 15, odd.

questions.q: Can 14 kids make 2 equal teams?

days.guide: Give the 12-item Unit 9 test.

questions.q: Is 22 odd or even?
questions.a: Even.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test (suggested 12): 1) 15 → odd 2) 22 → even 3) 16 = 8 + 8 4) 3 rows of 4 → 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 5) 5 rows of 3 → 15 6) 2 rows of 5 → 10, even 7) draw 4 + 4 + 4 → 3 rows of 4 8) arrays for 12: 1 by 12, 2 by 6, 3 by 4 (and turned versions) 9) 4 rows of 5 trees → 20 10) 3 bags of 5 apples → 15 11) 3 rows of 5 → 15, odd 12) 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8, even. Proficient: 10/12.

weeks.prep: Geoboard or dot paper, pattern blocks (or paper cutouts), straws with clay or pipe-cleaner connectors.
misconceptions: Thinking a turned square is no longer a square ('it's a diamond'). Turn it back and count equal sides and square corners.
Thinking only the pattern-block hexagon is a hexagon. Any closed shape with 6 straight sides is a hexagon.

days.guide: Sort pattern blocks and cutouts by number of sides and angles. Name the groups: triangle (3), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6).

questions.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
A shape has 5 angles. What is it?
questions.a: A pentagon.

days.guide: Make a square, rectangle, rhombus, and trapezoid on a geoboard. List what they share (4 sides, 4 angles).

questions.q: What do all quadrilaterals have?
questions.a: 4 sides and 4 angles (corners).

questions.q: How is a rhombus different from a square?
questions.a: A rhombus has 4 equal sides but does not need square corners.

days.guide: Read a clue; the child draws a shape that fits.

questions.q: Draw a quadrilateral with no square corners.
questions.a: Example: a slanted rhombus or a trapezoid with slanted sides.

questions.q: Draw a shape with 5 sides.
questions.a: Any closed pentagon.

days.guide: Build shapes with straws and connectors; count sides and vertices (corners).

questions.q: How many vertices does a triangle have?
A shape has 4 sides. How many vertices?

days.guide: Give the 10-item attribute quiz.

questions.q: 4 equal sides and 4 square corners?
questions.a: Square.

questions.q: 6 sides?
questions.a: Hexagon.

weeks.assessment_key: Shape quiz (suggested 10 clues): 1) 3 sides, 3 angles → triangle 2) 4 sides → quadrilateral 3) 5 sides → pentagon 4) 6 sides → hexagon 5) 4 equal sides, 4 square corners → square 6) 4 square corners, sides not all equal → rectangle 7) 4 equal sides, no square corners → rhombus 8) quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides → trapezoid 9) draw a shape with 5 sides → any closed pentagon 10) 6 vertices → hexagon. Proficient: 9/10.

weeks.prep: Dice, sugar cubes, boxes, grid paper, square tiles.
misconceptions: Counting only the faces you can see on a cube (3). Turn it to count all 6.
Drawing uneven rows when partitioning. Use grid paper to make same-size squares.

days.guide: Examine a die. Count faces (6), edges (12), and vertices (8), marking each with a sticker or pencil dot as you count.

questions.q: How many faces does a cube have?
How many edges and vertices?
questions.a: 12 edges, 8 vertices.

days.guide: Hunt for 3-D shapes at home (cubes, boxes, cans, balls) and record which have square faces.

questions.q: Does a soup can have square faces?
questions.a: No — its flat faces are circles.

questions.q: Does every box have square faces?
questions.a: No — many boxes have rectangle faces; only a cube-shaped box has all square faces.

days.guide: Cover a rectangle with square tiles, no gaps or overlaps; draw lines for rows and columns and count.

questions.q: A rectangle is covered by 2 rows of 5 tiles. How many tiles?
Why no gaps or overlaps?
questions.a: So every part is covered exactly once and the count is correct.

days.guide: Partition rectangles into 2 rows of 4, 3 rows of 3, etc. on paper and connect to repeated addition.

questions.q: 3 rows of 3 squares: total and addition?
2 rows of 4?

days.guide: Give the quiz on cube attributes and 6 partitioning problems.

questions.q: 4 rows of 4 squares: total?
How many vertices on a cube?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): cube — 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices, every face a square. Partition-and-count: 1) 2 rows of 4 → 8 squares 2) 3 rows of 3 → 9 3) 2 rows of 5 → 10 4) 4 rows of 2 → 8 5) 3 rows of 5 → 15 6) 4 rows of 4 → 16. Proficient: 8/9.

weeks.prep: Paper circles and rectangles, scissors, play dough, crackers or tortillas.
misconceptions: Calling any 2 pieces 'halves.' Halves must be equal in size.
Thinking equal shares must look the same. Show fourths of a square as 4 small squares and as 4 triangles — each is still one-fourth.

days.guide: Fold paper rectangles and circles in half different ways (lengthwise, crosswise, diagonally). Decide which folds make equal shares.

questions.q: Is a rectangle cut into 2 unequal pieces cut into halves?
questions.a: No — halves must be equal.

questions.q: How many halves make a whole?

days.guide: Cut play-dough pizzas and paper rectangles into thirds and fourths; label each piece.

questions.q: How many thirds make a whole?
If a pizza is cut into 4 equal pieces, what is each piece called?
questions.a: A fourth (a quarter).

days.guide: Cut 3 identical squares into fourths different ways (4 small squares, 4 strips, 4 triangles). Explain why each piece is still a fourth.

questions.q: A square cut into 4 triangles and another into 4 small squares: are all the pieces fourths?
questions.a: Yes — each is 1 of 4 equal parts of the same-size whole.

questions.q: Do equal shares need to be the same shape?
questions.a: No, only the same size.

days.guide: Share a tortilla or sandwich equally among 2, 3, or 4 people and describe the shares.

questions.q: If 3 people share a tortilla equally, what does each get?
questions.a: A third of the tortilla.

questions.q: More people sharing the same tortilla: bigger or smaller pieces?
questions.a: Smaller pieces.

days.guide: Give the Unit 10 test.

questions.q: Shade half of a rectangle.
questions.a: 1 of 2 equal parts shaded.

questions.q: How many fourths make a whole?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 10 test (suggested 12): 1) 3 sides → triangle 2) 6 sides → hexagon 3) 4 sides → quadrilateral 4) 5 sides → pentagon 5) rectangle in 2 rows of 3 → 6 squares 6) 3 rows of 4 → 12 squares 7) shade half of a circle (1 of 2 equal parts) 8) show thirds of a rectangle (3 equal parts) 9) show fourths of a square (4 equal parts) 10) choose the picture with equal shares (equal-size parts) 11) a pizza cut into 4 equal pieces: each is a fourth 12) 2 halves make a whole. Proficient: 10/12.

weeks.prep: Fact cards, base-ten blocks, and the fluency graph from Weeks 1 and 4. Write 12 within-100 and 10 within-1,000 problems.
misconceptions: Rushing facts and making careless errors. Focus on accuracy first, then speed.
Choosing the wrong operation in two-step problems. Have the child explain what each step finds.

days.guide: Give the 40-fact quiz and graph the score next to the baseline. Talk about the growth.
Solve 12 mixed problems within 100; the child explains one strategy aloud.
Solve 10 mixed problems within 1,000, drawing quick pictures where needed.
Solve 4 two-step stories and write one of your own.

questions.q: 120 stickers. Gave away 35, bought 50. How many now?
A farm had 200 eggs, sold 75, then collected 40. How many now?

days.guide: Complete a self-check (place value, fact families, regrouping) and mark two topics to practice next week.

questions.q: What is the value of the 6 in 562?
Write the fact family for 5, 8, 13.

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency quiz: score out of 40, graphed beside earlier scores (growth expected; 36+ shows mastery). Mixed problems (suggested): 54 + 29 = 83; 81 − 37 = 44; 345 + 278 = 623; 702 − 456 = 246; two-step: 120 stickers, gave away 35, bought 50 → 135. Proficient: about 85% correct and a clear explanation.

weeks.prep: Rulers, coins, a clock, graph paper. Prepare 15 mixed review items for Friday.
misconceptions: Measuring from 1 instead of 0. Check the starting point every time.
Counting coins in random order. Sort from greatest to least value first.

days.guide: Measure 5 objects in inches and cm; solve 2 compare-length problems.

questions.q: A pencil is 15 cm and a crayon is 9 cm. How much longer is the pencil?
questions.a: 6 cm.

questions.q: For the same pencil, which number is bigger: inches or cm?
questions.a: Centimeters.

days.guide: Count coin sets and tell time at 6 moments today; solve 3 money problems.

questions.q: 2 quarters and 1 dime?
The minute hand is on 3 and the hour hand just past 2. Time?

days.guide: Survey family about favorite summer activity, make a bar graph, and write 3 questions about it.

questions.q: Swim 6, bike 4. How many more chose swim?
What must a bar graph have?
questions.a: A title, labels, and a scale starting at 0 with equal spaces.

days.guide: Draw shapes from clues and partition shapes into equal shares.

questions.q: Draw a shape with 4 sides and 4 square corners.
questions.a: A square or rectangle.

questions.q: Divide a circle into thirds.
questions.a: 3 equal parts.

days.guide: Give 15 mixed items across measurement, data, and geometry.

questions.q: How many faces on a cube?

weeks.assessment_key: Mixed review (suggested 15): 1) measure a 6 cm line → 6 cm 2) measure a 3 in line → 3 in 3) 12 in − 8 in = 4 in 4) 2 quarters + 1 dime = 60¢ 5) $1 − 35¢ = 65¢ 6) clock showing 4:45 → 4:45 / quarter to 5 7) bar graph: 9 − 5 = 4 more 8) line plot: most common value is the tallest stack 9) triangle → 3 sides 10) hexagon → 6 sides 11) cube → 6 faces 12) halves → 2 equal parts 13) 3 rows of 4 → 12 14) fourths of a circle → 4 equal parts 15) 25 cm + 30 cm = 55 cm. Proficient: 13/15.

weeks.prep: Print or write the year-end test (two parts), poster board, markers, glue, and photos or drawing paper.
misconceptions: Getting stuck and leaving the rest blank. Remind the child to do what they know first, then return.
Posters with pictures but no math. Each picture needs a label with numbers and an equation.

days.guide: Give part 1 of the year-end test. Read instructions aloud but not answers.
Give part 2: measurement, graphs, money, time, shapes, and equal shares.

questions.q: 3 quarters + 2 dimes?
The minute hand is on 7 and the hour hand is past 8. Time?

days.guide: Plan a 'Math in My Home' poster with an array (egg carton), a measurement (a table), money (a price), and a graph.

questions.q: What array could you show from home?
questions.a: Example: an egg carton with 2 rows of 6 = 12.

questions.q: Name one measurement you could add.
questions.a: Example: the kitchen table is 48 inches long.

days.guide: Finish the poster with labeled pictures and practice explaining each idea aloud in about 3 minutes.

questions.q: Explain your array.
questions.a: Example: 'This muffin tin has 3 rows of 4, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 cups.'

questions.q: Why label pictures with numbers?
questions.a: So people can see the math in each picture.

days.guide: The child presents the poster to family; review the fluency growth graph from the year together.

questions.q: How did your fluency scores change this year?
questions.a: Answer from the graph — scores should rise from the Week 1 baseline.

questions.q: What math idea are you most proud of?
questions.a: Any specific answer with an example.

weeks.assessment_key: Year-end test part 1 (suggested): 1) 467 = 400 + 60 + 7 2) 528 < 582 3) 58 + 37 = 95 4) 90 − 46 = 44 5) 356 + 278 = 634 6) 600 − 245 = 355 7) 45 stickers, gave away 18, got 20 more → 47. Part 2: 8) measure lines (accept ±1 unit) 9) answer graph questions from the given bar graph and line plot 10) 3 quarters + 2 dimes = 95¢ 11) clock reading 8:35 12) 5 sides → pentagon 13) shade one fourth. Math fair rubric: 4 = arrays, a measurement, money, and a graph each shown with correct numbers and clearly explained in about 3 minutes; 3 = all shown, minor errors; 2 = 2–3 ideas; 1 = 1 idea.

SCI.overview: Teach science about 30–45 minutes a day, mostly hands-on: the child observes, predicts, tests, and records everything in a science notebook. Before each investigation, ask 'What do you predict?' and afterward 'What is your evidence?' Keep tests fair (change one thing at a time), handle heat, ovens, and outdoor water with an adult, and let failed designs become chances to improve.

weeks.prep: Buy a composition notebook and gather a magnifying glass, ruler, kitchen scale, and a bag for collecting. Plan a short outdoor walk to collect 5 natural objects (leaves, rocks, shells, sticks, seed pods).
misconceptions: Mixing observations with opinions ('the rock is pretty'). An observation uses the senses and can be checked by anyone ('the rock is gray and rough'); an opinion is what someone thinks or likes.
Asking questions that can't be tested ('Why is the leaf beautiful?'). Testable questions can be answered by measuring or trying something ('Which leaf is longest?').

days.guide: Help the child decorate the notebook cover, number the pages, and make a table of contents. Talk about what scientists do (observe, ask questions, test, record). The child draws and labels a magnifying glass (lens, handle).

questions.q: What do scientists do?
questions.a: They observe carefully, ask questions, test ideas, and record what they find.

questions.q: What does a magnifying glass do?
questions.a: Its lens makes small things look bigger so you can see details.

days.guide: Collect 5 natural objects outside. Model using the magnifier and describing words. The child records color, shape, texture, and size in a chart.

questions.q: Describe a rock using your senses.
questions.a: Example: It is gray with white specks, rough on one side, smooth on the other, and about as big as my thumb.

questions.q: Which sense do you use to describe texture?
questions.a: Touch.

days.guide: Brainstorm questions about the objects. Sort them into 'can test' and 'can't test.' The child writes 3 testable questions.

questions.q: Is 'Which rock is heaviest?' testable? Why?
questions.a: Yes — you can weigh the rocks and compare.

questions.q: Is 'Which shell is the nicest?' testable?
questions.a: No — it is an opinion.

days.guide: Measure each object's length with a ruler and weigh it on the kitchen scale. Order them by size and weight.

questions.q: Is the longest object always the heaviest?
questions.a: No — a long leaf can weigh less than a short rock; you have to measure both.

questions.q: What tool measures weight?
questions.a: A scale.

days.guide: The child shares observations aloud and explains observation vs. opinion with examples.

questions.q: Is 'The leaf has jagged edges' an observation or opinion?
questions.a: Observation.

questions.q: Is 'Rocks are boring' an observation or opinion?
questions.a: Opinion.

weeks.assessment_key: Observation chart (3 = proficient): 5 objects each with color, shape, texture, and size recorded using describing words or measurements, plus a labeled drawing. Testable questions: 3 questions that can be answered by measuring, comparing, or doing a test (e.g., 'Which rock is heaviest?', 'Does the shell sink or float?', 'Which leaf is longest?'). Not acceptable: opinion questions like 'Which rock is prettiest?'

weeks.prep: Gather a can opener, clothespin, zipper (on a jacket), paper, tape, paper clips, index cards, pennies, and 5 pencils. Write the design steps on a card: ask, imagine, plan, create, improve.
misconceptions: Building before planning. Remind: engineers ask questions and sketch first.
Thinking a design 'failed.' Testing shows what to improve — that's part of the process.

days.guide: Look at a can opener, clothespin, and zipper. Ask what problem each solves. The child records 3 in the notebook.

questions.q: What problem does a clothespin solve?
questions.a: It holds things like wet clothes or papers together so they don't fall or blow away.

questions.q: What problem does a zipper solve?
questions.a: It closes a jacket or bag quickly and keeps it shut.

days.guide: Present the problem: pencils keep rolling off the table. The child asks questions and lists what a solution must do (hold 5 pencils, not roll, use paper and tape).

questions.q: Why do pencils roll?
questions.a: They are round (or six-sided) and roll on a smooth surface when pushed.

questions.q: What must the pencil holder do?
questions.a: Hold the pencils so they don't roll off the table.

days.guide: Sketch two pencil-holder designs from paper and tape and label how the shape keeps pencils from rolling.

questions.q: What shape would stop pencils from rolling?
questions.a: A cup or a box with sides, or a tray with raised edges.

questions.q: Why label a sketch?
questions.a: So others understand what each part is and does.

days.guide: Build the best design and test it with 5 pencils. Record results and one improvement.

questions.q: If 2 pencils fell out, what could you improve?
questions.a: Make the walls taller or the base wider.

questions.q: Why test with the same 5 pencils each time?
questions.a: So the test is fair.

days.guide: The child explains the design steps (ask, imagine, plan, create, improve) using the pencil holder as the example.

questions.q: What happens in the 'improve' step?
questions.a: You change the design to make it work better and test again.

questions.q: Which step comes first?
questions.a: Ask — figure out the problem.

weeks.assessment_key: Design sketch (3 = proficient): two labeled sketches showing materials and how the shape stops pencils from rolling (e.g., walls, a cup shape, or a flat bottom). Test results: number of pencils held without rolling (out of 5) recorded, plus one specific improvement (e.g., 'make the walls taller').

weeks.prep: Collect 15 household objects made of wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric, paper, and rubber (keep glass items handled by an adult), sorting trays, and a cloth bag for the mystery-bag game.
misconceptions: Confusing an object with its material (a 'spoon' is the object; metal is the material).
Thinking all metals are shiny or all plastics are bendy. Test each property rather than guessing.

days.guide: Find 15 objects and identify the material of each (wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric, paper, rubber).

questions.q: What is a spoon usually made of?
questions.a: Metal (some are plastic or wood).

questions.q: What material is a T-shirt made of?
questions.a: Fabric (cloth, often cotton).

days.guide: Describe each material's properties in a table: hard/soft, rough/smooth, bendy/stiff, shiny/dull.

questions.q: Name two properties of a rubber band.
questions.a: Stretchy (bendy) and soft.

questions.q: Name two properties of a metal spoon.
questions.a: Hard and shiny (also stiff and smooth).

days.guide: Sort the objects by material, then by a property (e.g., bendy/stiff). The child explains the rule for each sort.

questions.q: Can a wooden ruler and a metal ruler go in the same group?
questions.a: Yes, if sorting by a property like 'stiff' — they are different materials but both stiff.

questions.q: What is a sorting rule?
questions.a: The property or feature you use to decide which group each object goes in.

days.guide: Put objects in a bag; the child identifies them by touch and names texture and hardness.

questions.q: How can you tell fabric from metal by touch?
questions.a: Fabric is soft and bendy; metal is hard, cool, and stiff.

questions.q: Which sense do you use in the mystery bag?
questions.a: Touch.

days.guide: The child classifies 10 new objects by material and properties and justifies one aloud.

questions.q: Classify a glass jar.
questions.a: Glass; hard, smooth, see-through (transparent).

questions.q: Why is a cooking pot made of metal?
questions.a: Metal is strong, hard, and can be heated without melting or burning.

weeks.assessment_key: Classification table (3 = proficient): each object with correct material and at least 2 correct properties, e.g., spoon — metal, hard, smooth, shiny; sock — fabric, soft, bendy; pencil — wood, hard, stiff; eraser — rubber, soft, bendy; cup — plastic, hard or bendy, smooth; book — paper, bendy, dull. One justified sort aloud.

weeks.prep: Gather a paper towel, napkin, sponge, cloth, plastic wrap, foil, an eyedropper or spoon, water, cups, and a paper doll. Cut all materials into same-size squares.
misconceptions: Changing more than one thing (using more water on one material). A fair test keeps everything the same except the material.
Thinking 'absorbent' means 'waterproof.' Absorbent soaks up water; waterproof keeps water out.

days.guide: Plan a fair test: same amount of water, same size pieces. The child writes predictions for each material.

questions.q: What must stay the same in a fair test?
questions.a: The amount of water and the size of each material piece — only the material changes.

questions.q: Predict which will absorb most: sponge or foil.
questions.a: Sponge — it has holes that soak up water; foil absorbs none.

days.guide: Drop 10 drops of water on each material; observe and record in a table.

questions.q: What happened to water on the plastic wrap?
questions.a: It beaded up and stayed on top — plastic wrap doesn't absorb water.

questions.q: Which absorbed the most?
questions.a: Usually the paper towel or sponge.

days.guide: Test which materials keep a paper doll dry under drips (foil, plastic wrap, cloth, paper).

questions.q: Which materials kept the doll dry?
questions.a: Foil and plastic wrap (they are waterproof).

questions.q: Why did the paper doll under paper get wet?
questions.a: Paper absorbs water and lets it soak through.

days.guide: Make a bar graph of results and decide the best material for a raincoat and for cleaning a spill.

questions.q: Best material for cleaning a spill?
questions.a: Paper towel or sponge — they absorb water.

questions.q: Best material for a raincoat?
questions.a: Plastic — it is waterproof.

days.guide: The child writes a claim and evidence sentence.

questions.q: Finish: 'The best material for a raincoat is ___ because ___.'
questions.a: Plastic, because water stayed on top and didn't soak through in our test.

questions.q: What is evidence?
questions.a: Facts or data from your test that support your claim.

weeks.assessment_key: Data table: expected results — paper towel and sponge absorb the most; cloth and napkin some; plastic wrap and foil absorb none (water beads up). Waterproof test: foil and plastic wrap keep the doll dry; cloth and paper let water through. Bar graph: labeled axes, bars match data. Claim-evidence sentence: 'The best material for a raincoat is plastic wrap (or foil) because no water got through it in our test.'

weeks.prep: Cut same-size strips (about 3 cm × 20 cm) of paper, foil, fabric, and plastic bag; gather a paper cup, string or a hole punch, pennies, cardboard, craft sticks, rubber bands, and a ruler.
misconceptions: Thinking thicker always means stronger. Test it — a thin plastic bag strip can hold more than a thicker paper strip.
Stretching rubber bands toward faces. Safety: point away and stretch gently.

days.guide: Hang a paper cup from each strip and add pennies until it breaks. Record the count.

questions.q: Which strip held the most pennies?
questions.a: Answer from data — often fabric or plastic.

questions.q: Why add pennies one at a time?
questions.a: To get an exact count of how much it held.

days.guide: Bend cardboard, plastic, craft sticks, and foil; rank from most to least flexible.

questions.q: Which is most flexible: foil or a craft stick?
questions.a: Foil.

questions.q: What does flexible mean?
questions.a: Able to bend without breaking.

days.guide: Stretch rubber bands and fabric strips; measure how far each stretches with a ruler.

questions.q: Which stretched farther: rubber band or fabric?
questions.a: The rubber band.

questions.q: What happens when you let go of a rubber band?
questions.a: It snaps back to its shape — it is elastic.

days.guide: Use data to choose the best material for a bag handle, a bridge deck, and a hair tie; explain with numbers.

questions.q: Why choose a rubber band for a hair tie?
questions.a: It stretches and goes back to its shape.

questions.q: Why choose the strongest strip for a bag handle?
questions.a: It held the most pennies, so it can carry heavy things.

days.guide: Present results in a chart and answer 'Why do engineers test materials?'

questions.q: Why do engineers test materials?
questions.a: To find the best material for a job so things work and are safe.

questions.q: What would happen if a bridge used a weak material?
questions.a: It could bend or break.

weeks.assessment_key: Strength chart: number of pennies each strip held before breaking (fabric and plastic bag usually hold the most; paper and foil fewer). Material choices: bag handle — strongest strip from data (often fabric or plastic) because it held the most pennies; bridge deck — a stiff, strong material such as craft sticks or cardboard; hair tie — rubber band because it stretches and snaps back. Explanations must use numbers from the data.

weeks.prep: Gather same-size ice cubes, small cups or plates, foil, cloth, newspaper, bubble wrap, rubber bands, and a timer. Start early in the day — melting may take a few hours.
misconceptions: Thinking a coat 'makes heat' or that foil keeps ice 'cold' by itself. Insulators slow heat from moving in or out.
Checking cubes at different times. Check all at the same time every 15 minutes.

days.guide: The child predicts which wrapper (foil, cloth, newspaper, bubble wrap, none) will keep ice from melting longest.

questions.q: Which cube do you predict will melt first?
questions.a: The one with no wrapper.

questions.q: Why include a cube with no wrapper?
questions.a: To compare — it shows what happens without an insulator.

days.guide: Wrap identical ice cubes and check every 15 minutes; record observations and melt time.

questions.q: Why use identical ice cubes?
questions.a: So the test is fair; only the wrapper changes.

questions.q: What makes ice melt?
questions.a: Heat from the warm air moves into the ice.

days.guide: Design and build an ice cube keeper from two materials and sketch it.

questions.q: Why might two layers work better than one?
questions.a: More layers (and trapped air) slow heat moving in.

questions.q: Which materials would you combine?
questions.a: Example: bubble wrap inside and cloth outside.

days.guide: Test the keeper against the best single material and compare.

questions.q: If your keeper lasted longer, what does that show?
questions.a: Your design was a better insulator.

questions.q: Name a weakness to fix.
questions.a: Example: gaps let warm air in.

days.guide: Write a conclusion about which materials make good insulators and why.

questions.q: What is an insulator?
questions.a: A material that slows heat from moving through it.

questions.q: Why do we wear coats in winter?
questions.a: Coats are insulators that slow our body heat from escaping.

weeks.assessment_key: Data comparison: the unwrapped cube melts first; cloth, newspaper, and bubble wrap slow melting (bubble wrap or layered newspaper often last longest, depending on wrapping). Proficient: data recorded every 15 minutes for each cube, the keeper's time compared with the best single material, and a strength/weakness named. Conclusion: good insulators (cloth, newspaper, bubble wrap, trapped air) slow heat from moving into the ice.

weeks.prep: Gather craft sticks, straws, foil, a plastic bag, fabric, tape, a spray bottle, a small toy, and the Unit 2 data. Prepare a short properties quiz (8 items).
misconceptions: Choosing materials by looks. Use test data: which materials were waterproof and strong?
Changing several things when improving. Change one part, then retest.

days.guide: Define the problem: design a mini umbrella to keep a toy dry. List criteria: waterproof, sturdy, light.

questions.q: What are criteria?
questions.a: What the design must do to be successful.

questions.q: Why must the umbrella be waterproof?
questions.a: To keep water from getting through to the toy.

days.guide: Use earlier test data to choose materials and sketch a labeled design.

questions.q: Which canopy material does your data support?
questions.a: Plastic bag or foil — they were waterproof.

questions.q: Which material could make a sturdy handle?
questions.a: A craft stick or straw.

days.guide: Build the umbrella and test it under a spray bottle for 30 seconds.

questions.q: Why spray for exactly 30 seconds?
questions.a: To test fairly every time.

questions.q: How do you know if it worked?
questions.a: The toy stays dry.

days.guide: Improve one part and retest; record how the change affected results.

questions.q: If water dripped off the edges onto the toy, what could you change?
questions.a: Make the canopy wider.

questions.q: Why change only one part?
questions.a: So you know which change made the difference.

days.guide: Present the umbrella and explain material choices; give the properties quiz.

questions.q: Why is fabric a poor choice for the canopy?
questions.a: Fabric can absorb water and let it soak through.

questions.q: Name a property of foil.
questions.a: Waterproof (also shiny and bendy).

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (3 = proficient): explains criteria (waterproof, sturdy, light), names materials and cites earlier test data (e.g., 'plastic was waterproof in our drip test'), reports spray-test result and one improvement. Properties quiz (suggested 8): 1) foil — waterproof, shiny, bendy 2) sponge — absorbent, soft 3) craft stick — stiff, hard (wood) 4) rubber band — stretchy 5) glass — hard, see-through 6) fabric — soft, bendy 7) plastic wrap — waterproof, see-through 8) which is best for a raincoat? plastic.

weeks.prep: Gather 20 building blocks or LEGO bricks, craft sticks, paper and pencils, and photos (from books or online) of reused materials, like a table made from old fence boards or a building made from reused bricks.
misconceptions: Thinking the pieces become different materials when rebuilt. The same 20 pieces are still the same pieces — only the shape changes.
Losing count of pieces. Count and record each type before and after.

days.guide: Build a small house from 20 blocks and draw it. Count pieces of each type.

questions.q: How many blocks did you use?
Why count each type of piece?
questions.a: So you can check you use the same pieces later.

days.guide: Take the house apart and build a new object using the same 20 pieces. Draw it.

questions.q: Are these the same pieces?
questions.a: Yes — the same 20 blocks in a new shape.

questions.q: Did the blocks change?
questions.a: No, only how they are arranged.

days.guide: Compare the drawings and explain how the same pieces made different objects.

questions.q: How can the same pieces make a house and a car?
questions.a: By putting them together in a different arrangement.

questions.q: Did you have any pieces left over?
questions.a: Answer should be no if all 20 were used.

days.guide: Look at pictures of reused materials (old fence wood turned into a table, reused bricks). Discuss.

questions.q: How is a table made from old fence boards like your block build?
questions.a: The same pieces (boards) were taken apart and put together to make a new object.

questions.q: Why do people reuse materials?
questions.a: It saves resources and reduces waste.

days.guide: The child writes an evidence-based account with drawings.

questions.q: Finish: 'I know an object made of pieces can become a new object because…'
questions.a: …I used the same 20 blocks to build a house and then a car.

questions.q: What is your evidence?
questions.a: My two drawings and my piece count.

weeks.assessment_key: Written account (3 = proficient): 'I know an object made of pieces can become a new object because I built a house from 20 blocks and then used the same 20 blocks to build a car.' Includes drawings of both objects and the piece count matching (20 = 20).

weeks.prep: Gather ice cube trays, chocolate chips, zip bags, warm water, old crayon pieces (paper removed), a muffin tin with liners, and an oven. Safety: an adult handles the oven and hot crayon wax.
misconceptions: Thinking melted chocolate is a new substance. It is still chocolate — just in liquid form.
Thinking 'reversible' means it looks exactly the same. It means it can change back to its earlier state (a solid again), even if the shape is different.

days.guide: Freeze water in ice trays, then melt the cubes. Record water → ice → water.

questions.q: What happens to water in the freezer?
questions.a: It freezes into solid ice.

questions.q: Can ice turn back into water?
questions.a: Yes — when it warms, it melts.

days.guide: Melt chocolate chips in a bag in warm water, then cool them in the fridge. Observe shape change and reversal.

questions.q: What happened to the chocolate when heated?
questions.a: It melted into a liquid.

questions.q: What happened in the fridge?
questions.a: It became solid again, in a new shape.

days.guide: With an adult, melt crayon pieces in a muffin tin at low heat, then cool into new crayons.

questions.q: Are the new crayons still crayon wax?
questions.a: Yes — same material, new shape.

questions.q: Why must an adult help?
questions.a: The oven and melted wax are hot and can burn.

days.guide: Make a before/heated/cooled chart for the three investigations.

questions.q: What do all three have in common?
questions.a: Heating melted them and cooling made them solid again.

questions.q: What does reversible mean?
questions.a: A change that can be undone.

days.guide: The child explains which changes were reversible with evidence.

questions.q: Was melting chocolate reversible? Evidence?
questions.a: Yes — it became solid again in the fridge.

questions.q: Is freezing water reversible?
questions.a: Yes — ice melts back into water.

weeks.assessment_key: Before/heated/cooled chart: water — liquid → solid ice when cooled → liquid when warmed; chocolate — solid chips → liquid when heated → solid when cooled (new shape); crayons — solid pieces → liquid wax when heated → solid new crayon when cooled. Explanation: all three are reversible because the material went back to a solid when cooled; evidence from the chart.

weeks.prep: Gather eggs, bread and a toaster, pancake batter ingredients, and 12 picture cards (melting snow, baking a cake, freezing juice, burning wood, cooking an egg, melting butter, toasting bread, frying, freezing water, melting chocolate, burning a candle wick, popping popcorn). Safety: an adult handles the stove and toaster.
misconceptions: Thinking cooling undoes every heated change. A cooled cooked egg is still cooked.
Sorting by temperature instead of whether it can be undone. Ask 'Can it go back to how it was?'

days.guide: Observe a raw egg, then cook it with an adult. Discuss whether it can become raw again.

questions.q: Can a cooked egg become raw again?
questions.a: No — cooking is an irreversible change.

questions.q: How did the egg change?
questions.a: The clear liquid turned white and solid; the yolk got firm.

days.guide: Toast bread and compare to untoasted bread. Try to 'untoast' it by cooling, and record.

questions.q: Did cooling make the toast soft bread again?
questions.a: No — toasting can't be reversed.

questions.q: Describe the toast vs. bread.
questions.a: Toast is brown, hard, and crunchy; bread is soft and lighter.

days.guide: Make pancakes and describe how liquid batter becomes solid when heated.

questions.q: What happened to the batter in the pan?
questions.a: Heat turned the runny liquid into a solid pancake.

questions.q: Can the pancake turn back into batter?
questions.a: No.

days.guide: Sort 12 picture cards into reversible and irreversible.

questions.q: Is burning wood reversible?
questions.a: No — it turns into ash and smoke.

questions.q: Is freezing juice reversible?
questions.a: Yes — it melts back into juice.

days.guide: Write an argument: some heated changes can be reversed and some cannot, with two pieces of evidence each.

questions.q: Give evidence of a reversible heated change.
questions.a: Melted chocolate became solid again when cooled.

questions.q: Give evidence of an irreversible heated change.
questions.a: A cooked egg stayed cooked when it cooled.

weeks.assessment_key: Change sort: reversible — melting snow, freezing juice, melting butter, freezing water, melting chocolate; irreversible — baking a cake, burning wood, cooking an egg, toasting bread, frying, burning a candle wick, popping popcorn. Argument (3 = proficient): claim stated; 2 reversible examples (ice melting/refreezing, chocolate) and 2 irreversible (egg, toast/pancake) with evidence from the week's tests.

weeks.prep: Collect clean recyclables (boxes, tubes, caps, egg cartons), glue, tape, scissors, a camera or drawing paper, and juice and ice-pop molds. Prepare an 8-item quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking a melted-and-refrozen ice pop is a completely different material. It is still frozen juice (reversible), though the shape may change.
Gluing so pieces can't come apart for the rebuild. Use tape where you plan to take it apart.

days.guide: Plan a new object (toy, organizer) from recyclables and sketch it.

questions.q: What object will you build?
questions.a: Example: a pencil organizer from tubes and a box.

questions.q: Why sketch first?
questions.a: To plan which pieces go where.

days.guide: Build the object, count pieces used, and label parts.

questions.q: How many tubes did you use?
questions.a: Answer from count.

questions.q: What is each part for?
questions.a: Example: tubes hold pencils; the box is the base.

days.guide: Disassemble and rebuild into a different object; draw or photograph both.

questions.q: Did you use the same pieces?
questions.a: Yes — same pieces, new object.

questions.q: How is this like the block house?
questions.a: Same pieces were rearranged into a new object.

days.guide: Freeze juice pops; let one melt and refreeze. Discuss if it's the same.

questions.q: Is the refrozen pop still juice?
questions.a: Yes — freezing and melting are reversible.

questions.q: What might be different?
questions.a: Its shape (it may not fit the mold shape).

days.guide: Give the unit quiz and have the child present the recycled builds.

questions.q: Is baking a cake reversible?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Is melting ice reversible?
questions.a: Yes.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation: shows 2 different objects from the same recyclables with piece counts. Unit quiz (suggested 8): 1) Can the same blocks make a different object? Yes 2) Melting ice — reversible 3) Baking bread — irreversible 4) Freezing water — reversible 5) Burning paper — irreversible 6) Melting crayons and cooling — reversible 7) Cooking an egg — irreversible 8) A refrozen ice pop is still juice — reversible change.

weeks.prep: Gather a weed with roots (ask before pulling), a celery stalk with leaves, a glass, food coloring, bean seeds, paper towels, zip bags, and tape. Start the bean bag early in the week.
misconceptions: Thinking plants eat soil for food. Plants make their own food using sunlight; roots take in water and minerals.
Thinking stems are just for holding up the plant. Stems also carry water from roots to leaves.

days.guide: Dig up a weed and identify roots, stem, leaves, and flowers. Draw and label it.

questions.q: What do roots do?
questions.a: Hold the plant in the ground and take in water.

questions.q: What do leaves do?
questions.a: Use sunlight to make food for the plant.

days.guide: Put celery in colored water and observe over a day.

questions.q: Predict what will happen to the celery.
questions.a: The colored water will move up the stem into the leaves.

questions.q: What does this show?
questions.a: The stem carries water up the plant.

days.guide: Plant bean seeds in wet paper towels in a zip bag on a window.

questions.q: What part grows first from a bean seed?
questions.a: The root.

questions.q: Why keep the towel wet?
questions.a: Seeds need water to sprout.

days.guide: List what plants need and write questions to test.

questions.q: What do plants need?
questions.a: Water, light, air, space, and nutrients from soil.

questions.q: Write a testable question.
questions.a: Do plants need light to grow?

days.guide: Record observations of celery and bean bag; explain the stem's job.

questions.q: Explain the stem's job.
questions.a: It carries water from the roots to the leaves and holds the plant up.

questions.q: What did you see in the celery leaves?
questions.a: The color of the water.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeled drawing: roots (take in water, hold plant), stem (carries water, holds plant up), leaves (make food using sunlight), flower (makes seeds). Observation log: dated entries showing colored water moving up celery (colored lines and leaf edges) and bean roots appearing first, then a shoot. Explanation: the stem carries water from roots to leaves.

weeks.prep: Get 4 similar bean seedlings in cups (from last week's bag planted in soil or sprouted earlier), a dark closet, a ruler, a watering cup, and a data table. Label cups LIGHT 1, LIGHT 2, DARK 1, DARK 2.
misconceptions: Watering the plants different amounts. Only light should change.
Expecting dark plants to die instantly. Plants in the dark often grow tall, thin, and pale/yellow at first as they stretch for light.

days.guide: Plan a fair test: 2 plants in light, 2 in a dark closet, same water and soil. Write predictions.

questions.q: What is the one thing we change?
questions.a: Light.

questions.q: What do we keep the same?
questions.a: Water, soil, cup size, and type of plant.

days.guide: Set up four plants, label cups, and measure starting heights in cm.

questions.q: Why measure the starting height?
questions.a: To compare growth later.

questions.q: Why use 2 plants in each group?
questions.a: In case one plant is different — more plants make results more reliable.

days.guide: Measure height and note leaf color and stem shape; record in the data table.

questions.q: What do you measure from?
questions.a: The soil line to the top of the plant.

questions.q: Why record color?
questions.a: Color shows plant health.

days.guide: Draw both groups and compare color and stem shape.

questions.q: What color are the dark plants' leaves?
questions.a: Pale or yellow.

questions.q: Why do they lose color?
questions.a: Plants need light to make food and stay green.

days.guide: Explain why only light was changed and what we keep the same.

questions.q: Why change only one thing?
questions.a: So we know the light caused any difference.

questions.q: What is a fair test?
questions.a: A test where only one thing changes.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan: question (Do plants need light?), prediction, variable changed (light), kept the same (water, soil, cup, plant type), measurement (height in cm). Data table with dated heights and leaf color. Expected: light plants stay green and sturdy; dark plants turn pale/yellow with thin, stretched or droopy stems.

weeks.prep: Get 4 more seedlings (2 watered, 2 not), a measuring cup, ruler, and graph paper. Continue measuring the light-test plants.
misconceptions: Overwatering 'watered' plants. Give the same small measured amount each time.
Graphing without a title or labels. Every graph needs a title, labels, and a scale.

days.guide: Set up 2 watered and 2 unwatered plants in the same light. Predict results.

questions.q: What is changed in this test?
questions.a: Water.

questions.q: Predict the unwatered plants.
questions.a: They will wilt and stop growing.

days.guide: Measure the light-test plants and graph height over time.

questions.q: What does the graph show?
questions.a: How much each plant grew over time.

questions.q: Which group is greener?
questions.a: The light group.

days.guide: Observe the water-test plants: wilting, color, and height.

questions.q: What does wilting look like?
questions.a: Leaves and stems droop and become soft.

questions.q: Why do plants wilt?
questions.a: They don't have enough water.

days.guide: Make bar graphs comparing plants with and without light and water.

questions.q: What goes on the bottom of the graph?
questions.a: The plant groups.

questions.q: What goes up the side?
questions.a: Height in centimeters.

days.guide: Share the graphs with a family member and explain which plants look healthiest and what surprised you.

questions.q: Which plants look healthiest?
questions.a: The ones with both light and water.

questions.q: What surprised you?
questions.a: Example: the dark plants grew tall but pale.

weeks.assessment_key: Two bar graphs (3 = proficient): titles, labeled axes (plant; height in cm), equal scale, bars that match data. Expected: watered plants taller and upright; unwatered plants wilted and drooping; light plants green, dark plants pale.

weeks.prep: Have all plant data, poster paper, and markers. Prepare a short quiz (6 items).
misconceptions: Writing a conclusion without evidence. Always include 'My evidence is…' with data.
Thinking a plant that wilts can never recover. Many recover if watered soon.

days.guide: Take final measurements and complete the data tables.

questions.q: Which plant grew tallest?
questions.a: Answer from data (usually a light-and-water plant).

questions.q: Why take final measurements?
questions.a: To see the full results.

days.guide: Write a conclusion: 'Plants need ___ and ___ to grow. My evidence is…'

questions.q: Complete the conclusion.
questions.a: Plants need light and water to grow. My evidence is the plants with both were tallest and greenest.

questions.q: What is evidence?
questions.a: Data that supports the claim.

days.guide: Move closet and unwatered plants to light and water; predict whether they recover.

questions.q: Predict whether the dark plant recovers.
questions.a: It may turn green again once in light, if not too weak.

questions.q: Why might some not recover?
questions.a: They went too long without what they needed.

days.guide: Make a poster of the investigation.

questions.q: What parts go on the poster?
questions.a: Question, prediction, test, results, conclusion.

questions.q: Why include a graph?
questions.a: To show the data clearly.

days.guide: Present the poster and give the quiz.

questions.q: What do plants need to grow?
questions.a: Light, water, air, and nutrients.

questions.q: What happens to plants without water?
questions.a: They wilt.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric (3 = proficient): question, prediction, test setup, results (graph), and conclusion: 'Plants need light and water to grow. My evidence is the plants with light and water were tallest and green; the ones in the dark turned pale and the ones without water wilted.' Quiz (suggested 6): 1) Plants need light, water, air, and nutrients 2) In a fair test you change one thing 3) A plant in the dark turns pale/yellow 4) A plant without water wilts 5) The stem carries water 6) Why use two plants per group? To make results more reliable.

weeks.prep: Collect assorted seeds (maple 'helicopters,' dandelion, burrs, acorns, apple and other fruit seeds), an old sock, a fan, and a tape measure. Check the walking area for poison oak or foxtails.
misconceptions: Thinking seeds move by themselves. They are carried by wind, water, animals, or fur, or pop out of pods.
Thinking animals plant seeds on purpose. Most dispersal is accidental (seeds stick or pass through).

days.guide: Collect seeds and sort by how they might travel.

questions.q: How do dandelion seeds travel?
questions.a: By wind — they have fluffy parachutes.

questions.q: How do burrs travel?
questions.a: They hook onto animal fur or clothes.

days.guide: Walk through grass with a sock over a shoe; count seeds that stick.

questions.q: Why did seeds stick to the sock?
questions.a: They have hooks or stickers that grab onto fur and cloth.

questions.q: How does this help plants?
questions.a: Seeds get carried to new places to grow.

days.guide: Use a fan to test which seeds travel farthest; measure distances.

questions.q: Which seed traveled farthest?
questions.a: Usually a light, fluffy seed like dandelion.

questions.q: Why do heavy seeds not go far in wind?
questions.a: They are too heavy for the wind to carry.

days.guide: Read about birds eating berries and dropping seeds; draw a seed's journey.

questions.q: How do birds spread seeds?
questions.a: They eat berries and the seeds pass through and drop in new places.

questions.q: Why do some plants have tasty fruit?
questions.a: Animals eat the fruit and carry the seeds away.

days.guide: Match 8 seeds to their dispersal method with reasons.

questions.q: How does a maple seed travel?
questions.a: Wind — its wings spin like a helicopter.

questions.q: How does a coconut travel?
questions.a: It floats on water.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching (suggested 8): dandelion — wind (fluffy parachute); maple — wind (wings spin); burr — animal fur (hooks); coconut — water (floats); berry — animals eat and drop seeds; acorn — squirrels bury them; apple seed — animals eat fruit; cocklebur/foxtail — sticks to fur or socks. Journey drawing: fruit eaten → seed carried → dropped → sprouts into new plant.

weeks.prep: Gather an old sock, pom-poms, Velcro, fabric scraps, pipe cleaners, a tray of seeds or rice, and tape.
misconceptions: Thinking any material will grab seeds. Test which surfaces (fuzzy, hooked) work best.
Counting differently each test. Use the same tray and same drag distance each time.

days.guide: Design a model 'animal' that picks up and carries seeds like fur; sketch two ideas.

questions.q: What feature of fur helps carry seeds?
questions.a: It is fuzzy and seeds' hooks catch in it.

questions.q: What materials could act like fur?
questions.a: Velcro, fuzzy fabric, pipe cleaners.

days.guide: Build the model following the sketch.

questions.q: Why follow your sketch?
questions.a: So you build what you planned.

questions.q: Which part will touch the seeds?
questions.a: The fuzzy or Velcro side.

days.guide: Drag the model through seeds and count those picked up and dropped.

questions.q: How many seeds stuck?
questions.a: Answer from count.

questions.q: Why count dropped seeds too?
questions.a: Dropping in new places is how seeds spread.

days.guide: Change the model's shape or material and retest.

questions.q: What did you change?
questions.a: Example: added more Velcro.

questions.q: Did more seeds stick?
questions.a: Answer from data.

days.guide: Explain how the model is like a real animal and how its shape helps.

questions.q: How is your model like a dog walking through a field?
questions.a: Both carry seeds stuck in fur to new places.

questions.q: Why does the shape matter?
questions.a: More surface area catches more seeds.

weeks.assessment_key: Model test data: seeds picked up and dropped counted for each version. Explanation (3 = proficient): 'My model is like a real animal's fur because the fuzzy/hooked surface catches seeds; as it moves, some seeds fall off in new places.'

weeks.prep: Gather a flower to dissect (lily or tulip works well), cheese puffs or colored chalk dust, paper flowers, cotton swabs, and a tally sheet. Note bee-sting allergies before observing pollinators outside.
misconceptions: Thinking bees visit flowers to help plants. They visit for nectar and pollen as food; pollination happens by accident.
Thinking only bees pollinate. Butterflies, hummingbirds, bats, moths, and wind also pollinate.

days.guide: Dissect a flower and find petals and pollen; draw and label.

questions.q: Where is pollen found?
questions.a: On the tips (anthers) inside the flower.

questions.q: What do petals do?
questions.a: Their colors and scents attract pollinators.

days.guide: Watch flowers outside for 15 minutes and tally visitors.

questions.q: Which pollinator did you see most?
questions.a: Answer from tally.

questions.q: Why do bees visit flowers?
questions.a: To get nectar and pollen for food.

days.guide: Dust fingers with cheese-puff powder and 'visit' paper flowers.

questions.q: What happened to the powder?
questions.a: It moved from flower to flower.

questions.q: What does the powder represent?
questions.a: Pollen.

days.guide: Read about bees, hummingbirds, and bats as pollinators; record one fact each.

questions.q: How do hummingbirds pollinate?
questions.a: Pollen sticks to their heads and beaks while they drink nectar.

questions.q: When do bats pollinate?
questions.a: At night.

days.guide: Explain why plants need pollinators and pollinators need plants.

questions.q: Why do plants need pollinators?
questions.a: To move pollen so they can make seeds.

questions.q: Why do pollinators need plants?
questions.a: For food — nectar and pollen.

weeks.assessment_key: Model explanation: dusty fingers (like a bee's body) picked up 'pollen' from one flower and left some on the next, showing how pollinators move pollen. Explanation (3 = proficient): 'Plants need pollinators to move pollen so they can make seeds; pollinators need plants for food (nectar and pollen).'

weeks.prep: Gather pipe cleaners, cotton balls, tape, craft sticks, powdered drink mix in two colors, and paper flowers with paper cups glued in the center. Prepare an 8-item unit quiz.
misconceptions: Only testing pick-up, not drop-off. A good pollinator tool must also leave powder on the next flower.
Thinking cotton always works best. Compare data from two designs.

days.guide: Design a hand pollinator tool that moves powder from flower to flower; sketch.

questions.q: What must the tool do?
questions.a: Pick up powder and drop it on another flower.

questions.q: Which material could act like bee hair?
questions.a: Cotton or pipe cleaner fuzz.

days.guide: Build the hand pollinator, shaping the tip to reach into a paper flower.

questions.q: Why shape the tip?
questions.a: So it reaches the pollen in the flower's center.

questions.q: What holds the parts together?
questions.a: Tape.

days.guide: Test how well it picks up and drops powder; record results.

questions.q: How do you know pollen moved?
questions.a: Colored powder from flower 1 appears on flower 2.

questions.q: Why use two colors?
questions.a: To see which flower the powder came from.

days.guide: Compare two designs and decide which works better.

questions.q: Which worked better and why?
questions.a: Answer from data, e.g., fuzzy pipe cleaner moved more powder.

questions.q: What would you improve?
questions.a: Example: add more cotton.

days.guide: Present the model and give the unit quiz.

questions.q: Name two ways seeds travel.
questions.a: Wind and animals (also water).

questions.q: What is pollination?
questions.a: Moving pollen from one flower to another so plants can make seeds.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation: tool design, test results (powder moved from flower 1 to flower 2), and why. Unit quiz (suggested 8): 1) Dandelion seeds travel by wind 2) Burrs travel on animal fur 3) Birds spread seeds by eating fruit 4) Coconut travels by water 5) Pollen moves from flower to flower 6) Bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, bats are pollinators 7) Plants need pollination to make seeds 8) Pollinators get food (nectar) from flowers.

weeks.prep: Gather a hula hoop or 1-meter string loop, magnifier, clipboard and tally sheet, and optionally the free Seek app. Choose two very different survey spots (a lawn or garden bed, and a sidewalk crack or gravel). Remind the child to look, not touch, unknown insects and plants; wash hands afterward.
misconceptions: Counting every ant as a new kind. Tally KINDS of living things (ants = 1 kind) for diversity.
Thinking a habitat is just 'where an animal lives.' A habitat must provide food, water, shelter, and space.

days.guide: Teach that a habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space. Walk around the block and list 4 small habitats with one animal each.

questions.q: What 4 things does a habitat provide?
questions.a: Food, water, shelter, and space.

questions.q: Name an animal that lives in a tree habitat.
questions.a: Examples: squirrel, bird, beetle.

days.guide: Lay the hoop on a lawn or garden bed; search for 15 minutes and tally different kinds of plants and animals.

questions.q: If you see 10 ants, how many kinds is that?
questions.a: 1 kind.

questions.q: Why use a hoop?
questions.a: To survey the same-size area fairly.

days.guide: Repeat the 15-minute hoop survey in a very different spot and tally the same way.

questions.q: Why survey for the same amount of time?
questions.a: So the comparison is fair.

questions.q: Predict which spot has more kinds.
questions.a: The spot with more plants, water, and shade.

days.guide: Make a bar graph comparing the number of kinds in each spot; circle organisms found in both.

questions.q: Which spot had more kinds of living things?
questions.a: Answer from data (usually the lawn/garden).

questions.q: What does 'diversity' mean?
questions.a: How many different kinds of living things are in a place.

days.guide: The child writes a claim with evidence and shares it aloud.

questions.q: Finish the claim.
questions.a: The garden spot had more kinds of living things because it had more plants and water.

questions.q: Why might the sidewalk crack have fewer kinds?
questions.a: It has little soil, water, food, and shelter.

weeks.assessment_key: Survey data: kinds of living things tallied for each spot. Bar graph with title, two labeled bars, and scale. Claim-evidence (3 = proficient): 'The garden spot had more kinds of living things because it had more plants, water, and shade,' supported by the counts (e.g., 9 kinds vs. 3 kinds).

weeks.prep: Get library books or National Geographic Kids articles on redwood forests, the Mojave Desert (e.g., A Walk in the Desert by Rebecca L. Johnson), and grasslands, plus a short grassland video. Make a three-column chart.
misconceptions: Thinking deserts have no life. Many plants and animals have adaptations to survive with little water.
Thinking a habitat with bigger animals has more diversity. Diversity is the number of kinds, not size.

days.guide: Read about a redwood forest; list 8 plants and animals and where each finds shelter.

questions.q: Name 2 animals that live in a redwood forest.
questions.a: Examples: banana slug, owl, deer, woodpecker.

questions.q: Where might an owl find shelter?
questions.a: In a hole in a tree.

days.guide: Read about the Mojave Desert and list living things; discuss how each survives with little water.

questions.q: How does a cactus survive with little water?
questions.a: It stores water in its thick stem and has spines instead of leaves.

questions.q: How does a desert tortoise survive the heat?
questions.a: It stays in a burrow underground during the hottest times.

days.guide: Watch a grassland video and list plants and animals; tally kinds named.

questions.q: What plants are most common in a grassland?
questions.a: Grasses (and wildflowers).

questions.q: Name a grassland animal.
questions.a: Examples: ground squirrel, hawk, coyote, bison (prairie).

days.guide: Make a three-column chart and a bar graph of the number of kinds; describe the pattern.

questions.q: Which habitat had the most kinds on your chart?
questions.a: Usually the forest.

questions.q: Why?
questions.a: More water and plants give more food and shelter.

days.guide: The child answers in 3–4 sentences which habitat has the most diversity and why.

questions.q: What helps a habitat have more diversity?
questions.a: More water, plants, and shelter.

questions.q: Why does the desert have fewer kinds?
questions.a: There is little water.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart: forest (e.g., redwood, fern, banana slug, owl, deer, squirrel, salamander, woodpecker), desert (Joshua tree, cactus, desert tortoise, roadrunner, lizard, kangaroo rat, jackrabbit), grassland (grasses, wildflowers, ground squirrel, hawk, coyote, gopher snake). Written answer (3 = proficient): names the habitat with the most kinds on the chart (usually the forest) and explains with evidence: more water and plants provide more food and shelter, so more animals can live there.

weeks.prep: Find the Monterey Bay Aquarium kelp forest live cam or a kelp video, a clear jar, magnifier, and pond-life photos. Safety: an adult goes along to collect pond water; don't drink it, and wash hands after.
misconceptions: Thinking kelp is a plant with roots. Kelp is a large algae with a holdfast that grips rocks (not roots).
Thinking tide pools are always underwater. They fill and empty with the tides.

days.guide: Watch the kelp forest cam or video for 10 minutes and list every kind of fish, plant, and animal.

questions.q: What animal wraps itself in kelp to rest?
questions.a: The sea otter.

questions.q: What does kelp provide for animals?
questions.a: Food and shelter.

days.guide: Scoop pond or puddle water into a clear jar with an adult, let it settle, and look for tiny swimmers; draw 3.

questions.q: What might you see in pond water?
questions.a: Tiny insects, worms, snails, or algae.

questions.q: Why let the water settle?
questions.a: So the mud sinks and you can see the living things.

days.guide: Read about California tide pools and sketch one with sea stars, anemones, crabs, and snails labeled.

questions.q: Where do anemones attach?
questions.a: To rocks.

questions.q: What happens to tide pools at low tide?
questions.a: The ocean water goes out, leaving pools of water between rocks.

days.guide: Add the water habitats to the chart and compare totals with land habitats.

questions.q: Which water habitat had the most kinds?
questions.a: Usually the kelp forest.

questions.q: Which habitat had the most kinds overall?
questions.a: Answer from the chart.

days.guide: The child tells a family member which habitat surprised them most, with two facts, and answers 2 questions.

questions.q: Give a fact about kelp.
questions.a: Kelp can grow very tall and fast, making an underwater forest.

questions.q: Give a fact about tide pools.
questions.a: Animals there must survive when the water goes out at low tide.

weeks.assessment_key: Updated chart: kelp forest (kelp, sea otter, rockfish, sea urchin, sea star, garibaldi), pond (algae, water insects, tadpoles, snails, duckweed), tide pool (sea star, anemone, crab, snail, mussel, barnacle). Oral explanation (3 = proficient): names the most surprising habitat and gives two accurate facts, answers 2 questions. Expected comparison: the kelp forest often shows the most kinds of living things in water.

weeks.prep: Gather a shoebox, construction paper, clay, twigs, sand, cotton, paint, and index cards. Help the child find 2 sources on the chosen habitat. Prepare an 8-item matching quiz.
misconceptions: Placing animals in the wrong habitat (a polar bear in the desert). Check each animal with a source.
Labels that only name the animal. Labels should tell what it eats and where it shelters.

days.guide: Choose a habitat and use 2 sources to list 6 living things and what each needs.

questions.q: Name 2 living things in a pond habitat.
questions.a: Examples: frog, duckweed, dragonfly.

questions.q: Why use 2 sources?
questions.a: To find more facts and check them.

days.guide: Paint or line the shoebox to show land, water, and sky; add plants.

questions.q: What would the background show for a desert?
questions.a: Sand, rocks, a bright sky, cactus.

questions.q: What would a kelp forest show?
questions.a: Water, tall kelp, a rocky sea floor.

days.guide: Model at least 4 animals and add labels telling what each eats and where it shelters.

questions.q: Write a label for a desert tortoise.
questions.a: Desert tortoise — eats grasses and plants; shelters in a burrow.

questions.q: Write a label for a sea otter.
questions.a: Sea otter — eats sea urchins, crabs, and clams; rests wrapped in kelp.

days.guide: Present the diorama, naming how many kinds of living things it shows, and compare with another habitat.

questions.q: Does your habitat have more or less diversity than the desert? Why?
questions.a: Answer with reasons (more water and plants = more kinds).

questions.q: What should a presenter do?
questions.a: Speak clearly and point to each part.

days.guide: Give the unit quiz.

questions.q: Where does a sea star live?
questions.a: Tide pool (rocky ocean shore).

questions.q: Where does a roadrunner live?
questions.a: Desert.

weeks.assessment_key: Diorama rubric (3 = proficient): habitat clearly shown (land, water, sky); at least 6 accurate living things including 4 animals; labels tell food and shelter; comparison with another habitat explained. Quiz (suggested 8): Joshua tree — desert; banana slug — redwood forest; sea otter — kelp forest; sea star — tide pool; tadpole — pond; roadrunner — desert; owl — forest; anemone — tide pool. Diversity question: the habitat with more water and plants has more kinds.

weeks.prep: Find before-and-after photos of Mount St. Helens (USGS) and a short passage about the 1980 eruption. Gather clay or play dough, a cup, baking soda, vinegar, a tray, blocks, marbles, damp soil, and photos of a California coastal landslide.
misconceptions: Thinking the baking-soda volcano is how real volcanoes work. Real eruptions are melted rock (magma) and gases from deep underground.
Thinking all Earth changes take a long time. Volcanoes, earthquakes, and landslides change land in minutes or hours.

days.guide: Compare before-and-after photos of Mount St. Helens and read about the 1980 eruption. Record how much the mountain changed in one day.

questions.q: How did Mount St. Helens change?
questions.a: The eruption blew off the top and north side, making it much shorter with a huge crater.

questions.q: How long did the change take?
questions.a: Minutes to hours (one day).

days.guide: Build a clay volcano, erupt it with baking soda and vinegar, and draw how the 'lava' changed the land.

questions.q: How is the model different from a real volcano?
questions.a: Real lava is melted rock that cools into new rock; the model is just foam.

questions.q: How can lava change land?
questions.a: It covers the land and hardens into new rock.

days.guide: Build a block tower on a tray resting on marbles and shake it. Read about a California earthquake.

questions.q: What happened to the tower when shaken?
questions.a: It wobbled or fell.

questions.q: How fast can an earthquake change roads?
questions.a: In seconds — it can crack or break roads.

days.guide: Pack damp soil on a tilted tray, pour water at the top, and time how fast it slides. Compare to landslide photos.

questions.q: What made the soil slide?
questions.a: Water made it heavy and slippery, and gravity pulled it down the slope.

questions.q: Is a landslide fast or slow?
questions.a: Fast — seconds to minutes.

days.guide: Fill a 3-row chart (event, how long, evidence and source).

questions.q: How long does an earthquake last?
questions.a: Usually seconds to a few minutes.

questions.q: What is your source for the volcano?
questions.a: Mount St. Helens photos and passage (USGS).

weeks.assessment_key: Fast-change chart (3 = proficient): Volcano — Mount St. Helens erupted on May 18, 1980; the top and side of the mountain blasted away in minutes to hours (it lost about 1,300 feet of height); source: USGS photos/passage. Earthquake — shaking lasts seconds to minutes and can crack roads and move ground; source: California earthquake reading. Landslide — soil and rock slide down a slope in seconds to minutes; source: model test and landslide photo. At least two sources named.

weeks.prep: Gather sugar cubes and a jar with a lid, two rough rocks, black paper, a magnifier, a small plastic container with a snap lid, a freezer, and Grand Canyon photos.
misconceptions: Thinking weathering and erosion are the same. Weathering breaks rock into pieces; erosion carries the pieces away.
Thinking slow changes don't happen because we can't see them. They happen over thousands to millions of years.

days.guide: Shake 5 sugar cubes in a jar for 2 minutes, then 2 more; compare corners.

questions.q: What happened to the sugar cube corners?
questions.a: They became rounder and broke off into crumbs.

questions.q: How is this like rocks in a river?
questions.a: Rocks bump together in moving water and wear down.

days.guide: Rub two rough rocks together over black paper for 2 minutes and look at the dust.

questions.q: How much dust did you make?
questions.a: Only a little.

questions.q: How long would it take to wear a rock away?
questions.a: A very long time — years and years.

days.guide: Read about how the Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon; look at rock layers and write 2 facts.

questions.q: What carved the Grand Canyon?
questions.a: The Colorado River.

questions.q: How long did it take?
questions.a: Millions of years.

days.guide: Fill a container with water, cap it, freeze overnight, and observe.

questions.q: What happened to the container?
questions.a: It bulged or cracked.

questions.q: Why?
questions.a: Water expands (takes more space) when it freezes into ice.

days.guide: The child writes 3 sentences explaining why weathering and erosion are slow, using evidence.

questions.q: How does ice crack rocks?
questions.a: Water gets into cracks, freezes, expands, and pushes the rock apart.

questions.q: What is erosion?
questions.a: Moving bits of rock and soil from one place to another by water, wind, or ice.

weeks.assessment_key: Observations: sugar cube corners got rounder and crumbs collected; rock rubbing made only a little dust; frozen water expanded and bulged or cracked the container. Written explanation (3 = proficient): 'Weathering and erosion change land slowly because only tiny bits break off at a time. The rocks made only a little dust after 2 minutes, and ice cracked the container a little — it takes millions of years to carve a canyon.'

weeks.prep: Make 12 picture cards (flood, eruption, canyon, earthquake, sand dune, landslide, glacier valley, rockfall, wave-worn cliff, river delta, mountain wearing down, mudslide). Get a long paper strip and two short sources on Yosemite Valley (glaciers and rockfalls).
misconceptions: Thinking a flood is slow. Floods happen in hours to days.
Placing events on the timeline by size, not time. Ask 'How long did it take?'

days.guide: Sort 12 cards into fast and slow and justify 3 aloud.

questions.q: Is a canyon fast or slow?
questions.a: Slow — it forms over millions of years.

questions.q: Is a landslide fast or slow?
questions.a: Fast.

days.guide: Make a timeline strip with seconds, hours, days, years, and millions of years; place each card.

questions.q: Where does an earthquake go?
questions.a: Seconds.

questions.q: Where does a glacier valley go?
questions.a: Thousands to millions of years.

days.guide: Read two sources about Yosemite Valley: glaciers carved it slowly; rockfalls happen in seconds.

questions.q: How did glaciers shape Yosemite Valley?
