questions.a: Huge, slow-moving ice scraped and carved the valley over a very long time.

questions.q: How fast is a rockfall?
questions.a: Seconds.

days.guide: Write a paragraph comparing one fast and one slow change.

questions.q: Name a fast and a slow change in Yosemite.
questions.a: Fast: rockfall. Slow: glaciers carving the valley.

questions.q: How do you know?
questions.a: From the sources (name them).

days.guide: Read the paragraph aloud, answer questions, and check each claim names a source.

questions.q: Why name a source?
questions.a: To show where your evidence came from.

questions.q: Is a flood fast or slow?
questions.a: Fast (hours to days).

weeks.assessment_key: Sort: fast — flood, eruption, earthquake, landslide, rockfall, mudslide; slow — canyon, sand dune, glacier valley, wave-worn cliff, river delta, mountain wearing down. Timeline: seconds (earthquake, rockfall), minutes–hours (landslide, eruption), days (flood), years (sand dune moving), millions of years (canyon, glacier valley). Paragraph (3 = proficient): compares one fast and one slow change with what happened, how long, and how we know (source named).

weeks.prep: Gather sand or soil in a long pan, a cup with a pinhole, a tray to catch water, Grand Canyon photos, poster paper, and markers. Prepare an 8-item quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking the sand model shows exactly how long canyons take. The model is much faster; the real canyon took millions of years.
Posters without evidence. Each event needs a source.

days.guide: Review notebook entries on fast and slow changes; highlight the strongest evidence for each.

questions.q: What is strong evidence for a fast change?
questions.a: Mount St. Helens before/after photos from one day.

questions.q: What is strong evidence for a slow change?
questions.a: The Grand Canyon took millions of years to carve.

days.guide: Tilt a pan of damp sand and let water trickle from a pinhole cup for 10 minutes; sketch every 2 minutes.

questions.q: What happened to the sand?
questions.a: Water carved a channel and carried sand downhill.

questions.q: Where did the sand go?
questions.a: It was deposited at the bottom of the pan.

days.guide: Compare the sand canyon to Grand Canyon photos: 2 alike, 1 different.

questions.q: How is the model like the Grand Canyon?
questions.a: Moving water carved a channel and carried material away.

questions.q: How is it different?
questions.a: The model took minutes; the real canyon took millions of years and is carved in rock.

days.guide: Make a 'Fast vs. Slow' poster with drawings, time labels, and one source for each event.

questions.q: What goes on each event card?
questions.a: Drawing, how long it takes, and a source.

questions.q: Is a glacier valley fast or slow?
questions.a: Slow.

days.guide: Give the unit quiz and have the child present the poster.

questions.q: Is an earthquake fast or slow?
questions.a: Fast.

questions.q: Explain one slow change.
questions.a: The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years.

weeks.assessment_key: Model comparison: alike — water carved a channel; sand washed downhill. Different — the model took 10 minutes, the real canyon millions of years (also: rock vs. sand). Unit quiz (suggested 8): earthquake — fast; canyon — slow; volcano eruption — fast; sand dune moving — slow; landslide — fast; glacier carving a valley — slow; flood — fast; rock weathering — slow. One explained with evidence.

weeks.prep: Gather sand and soil, a baking pan or tray, a watering can, drinking straws, newspaper, a ruler, and safety glasses for the wind test. Find photos of California cliff erosion (e.g., Pacifica).
misconceptions: Thinking erosion only removes land. Eroded material is deposited somewhere else.
Blowing toward someone's face during the wind test. Wear glasses and blow away from people.

days.guide: Build a sand hill, sprinkle it with water for 1 minute, and draw where sand was removed and deposited.

questions.q: Where did the sand go?
questions.a: Down the hill to the bottom.

questions.q: What is deposition?
questions.a: When moved sand or soil is dropped in a new place.

days.guide: Blow through a straw at a sand pile from 10 cm for 30 seconds and measure how far sand traveled.

questions.q: How far did the sand travel?
questions.a: Answer from measurement.

questions.q: How is this like real wind?
questions.a: Wind picks up and moves sand and soil, especially in dry places.

days.guide: Walk the neighborhood or a park and sketch or photograph erosion; note water or wind.

questions.q: What does exposed tree roots show?
questions.a: Soil was washed or blown away.

questions.q: What makes a gully?
questions.a: Running water carrying soil away.

days.guide: Read about California cliff erosion and look at photos; discuss why it's a problem.

questions.q: What erodes coastal cliffs?
questions.a: Ocean waves (and rain).

questions.q: Why is it a problem for people?
questions.a: Homes and roads near the edge can fall as cliffs wear away.

days.guide: Draw before-and-after pictures of the models and label erosion and deposit areas.

questions.q: Label the top of the hill after watering.
questions.a: Erosion — sand removed.

questions.q: Label the bottom of the hill.
questions.a: Deposit — sand dropped.

weeks.assessment_key: Before/after drawings (3 = proficient): water model shows sand removed from the top of the hill and deposited at the bottom; wind model shows sand moved away from the pile and deposited farther along the paper (distance measured in cm); erosion and deposit areas labeled.

weeks.prep: Prepare two trays of soil (one planted with grass seed two weeks earlier, or covered with moss), craft sticks, pebbles, a measuring cup, clear cups to catch runoff, and photos of retaining walls, windbreaks, levees, and sand fences.
misconceptions: Thinking a solution must stop erosion completely. Solutions slow erosion; compare how much each reduces it.
Using different amounts of water for each test. Use the same 2 cups each time.

days.guide: Look at photos of retaining walls, windbreaks, levees, and sand fences; write what each solves.

questions.q: What does a levee do?
questions.a: Holds back river water to prevent floods.

questions.q: What does a row of trees as a windbreak do?
questions.a: Slows wind so it blows away less soil.

days.guide: Pour 2 cups of water down bare soil and a grass tray; compare the runoff.

questions.q: Which runoff was muddier?
questions.a: The bare soil.

questions.q: Why did grass help?
questions.a: Roots hold the soil in place.

days.guide: Build a craft-stick wall and a pebble wall on a sand hill; test each with the same water.

questions.q: Which wall moved less sand?
questions.a: Answer from data.

questions.q: Why use the same water amount?
questions.a: To make it a fair test.

days.guide: Record all four tests in a table and rank least to most sand lost.

questions.q: Which lost the most?
questions.a: Bare soil.

questions.q: Which lost the least?
questions.a: Usually grass.

days.guide: Write which solution worked best and one weakness, using data.

questions.q: Weakness of planting grass?
questions.a: It takes time to grow.

questions.q: Weakness of a pebble wall?
questions.a: Water can flow between pebbles.

weeks.assessment_key: Data table ranking (typical): grass loses the least sand/soil (clearest runoff), then pebble wall, then craft-stick wall, and bare soil loses the most. Conclusion (3 = proficient): names the best solution (usually plants) with data as evidence and one weakness (e.g., grass takes weeks to grow).

weeks.prep: Gather a tray of sand, a small toy house or block, 10 craft sticks, foil, cloth, pebbles, clay, a measuring cup, and a ruler.
misconceptions: Testing designs with different hills. Rebuild the same hill shape before each test.
Ignoring constraints. Count materials before building.

days.guide: Define the problem: protect a toy house on a sand hill near a 'river'; list criteria and constraints.

questions.q: What is a constraint?
questions.a: A limit, like only 10 craft sticks.

questions.q: What is the criterion for success?
questions.a: The house stays put after 2 cups of water.

days.guide: Sketch two different solutions and label how each protects the house.

questions.q: How does a channel help?
questions.a: It directs water away from the house.

questions.q: How does a wall help?
questions.a: It blocks water from reaching the house.

days.guide: Build design 1, pour 2 cups of water, and measure house movement and sand loss.

questions.q: How far did the house move?
questions.a: Answer in cm.

questions.q: Where did the water go?
questions.a: Answer from observation.

days.guide: Rebuild the hill, build design 2, and test the same way.

questions.q: Why rebuild the same hill?
questions.a: To make the test fair.

questions.q: Which design did better?
questions.a: Answer from data.

days.guide: Compare designs in a T-chart and decide which to improve.

questions.q: Name a strength of your best design.
questions.a: Example: the house didn't move at all.

questions.q: Name a weakness.
questions.a: Example: water went around the wall.

weeks.assessment_key: Design sketches: two different, labeled solutions (e.g., wall vs. channel). T-chart (3 = proficient): strengths and weaknesses of each with data (how far the house moved in cm and how much sand washed away), and a decision about which to improve.

weeks.prep: Keep last week's designs and data; gather poster paper and markers. Find a short reading about dune grass protecting California beaches. Prepare 4 erosion photos and 3 situations for Friday.
misconceptions: Changing many features at once when improving. Change one feature and retest.
Presenting without data. Include numbers from tests.

days.guide: Change one feature of the better design and retest; record results.

questions.q: What did you change?
questions.a: Example: made the wall taller.

questions.q: Did it improve?
questions.a: Answer from data.

days.guide: Make a poster showing the problem, designs, data, and improved design.

questions.q: Why include data?
questions.a: To prove which design worked best.

questions.q: What is the problem?
questions.a: Water washing sand away from the house.

days.guide: Present the poster and answer 2 questions.

questions.q: Why did the improved design work better?
questions.a: Example: the taller wall blocked more water.

questions.q: What would you try next?
questions.a: Example: add plants.

days.guide: Read about dune grass protecting California beaches and compare to your designs.

questions.q: How does dune grass protect beaches?
questions.a: Its roots hold the sand and slow the wind.

questions.q: Which of your designs is most like dune grass?
questions.a: Example: adding 'plants' to the hill.

days.guide: Give the unit quiz.

questions.q: Best solution for a hillside washing away?
questions.a: Plant grass or shrubs — roots hold soil.

questions.q: Best solution for beach sand blowing away?
questions.a: Sand fences or dune grass.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric (3 = proficient): problem, both designs, test data, improved design with results. Unit quiz: erosion identified in 4 photos (e.g., gully, exposed roots, eroded cliff, washed-out path). Solutions: steep hillside soil washing away → plant grass/shrubs (roots hold soil); beach sand blowing away → sand fences or dune grass; river flooding a town → levee. Each with a reason.

weeks.prep: Gather photos of mountains, hills, valleys, plains, islands, and peninsulas; a California map; clay or play dough; a baking pan; water; and toothpick flags.
misconceptions: Confusing islands and peninsulas. An island has water all around; a peninsula has water on three sides and connects to land.
Thinking lakes and ponds are salty. Most lakes and ponds are fresh water; the ocean is salt water.

days.guide: Sort photos of landforms and write a one-line definition for each.

questions.q: What is a valley?
questions.a: Low land between hills or mountains.

questions.q: What is a peninsula?
questions.a: Land with water on three sides.

days.guide: Learn ocean, lake, river, pond, stream, bay and find California examples on a map.

questions.q: Name California's ocean.
questions.a: The Pacific Ocean.

questions.q: Name a California lake and river.
questions.a: Lake Tahoe; the Sacramento River.

days.guide: Build a clay landscape with a mountain, valley, island, and peninsula; add water.

questions.q: Where does the river flow?
questions.a: Downhill from the mountains to the ocean or lake.

questions.q: How do you make an island?
questions.a: Put land with water all around it.

days.guide: Label each feature with toothpick flags and photograph from above and from the side.

questions.q: Which view shows how tall the mountain is?
questions.a: The side view.

questions.q: Which view shows the shape of the lake?
questions.a: The view from above.

days.guide: Explain the model to a family member, pointing to each feature.

questions.q: How is a lake different from a river?
questions.a: A lake is still water surrounded by land; a river flows.

questions.q: How is an island different from a peninsula?
questions.a: An island is surrounded by water; a peninsula is attached to land.

weeks.assessment_key: Model labels: mountain, valley, island, peninsula, lake, river, ocean all correctly placed. Oral explanation (3 = proficient): points to each feature and tells how they differ (e.g., a mountain is much taller than a hill; a river flows, a lake is still; an island is surrounded by water; a peninsula is connected to land on one side).

weeks.prep: Get a California physical map, a blank California outline, colored pencils, and the bird's-eye photo of last week's model.
misconceptions: Thinking a map shows everything. Maps use symbols and colors from a key and show land from above.
Forgetting the compass rose. Maps need N, S, E, W.

days.guide: Study a physical map of California; mark the Sierra Nevada, Central Valley, Sacramento River, Lake Tahoe, and Pacific coast on a blank outline.

questions.q: Where are the Sierra Nevada mountains?
questions.a: In eastern California.

questions.q: What ocean is along California's west coast?
questions.a: The Pacific Ocean.

days.guide: Create a map key with colors and symbols for mountains, valleys, rivers, lakes, and ocean.

questions.q: What color usually shows water on maps?
questions.a: Blue.

questions.q: Why does a map need a key?
questions.a: To explain what the colors and symbols mean.

days.guide: Use the bird's-eye photo to draw a map of the model with a key and compass rose.

questions.q: What does a compass rose show?
questions.a: Directions: north, south, east, west.

questions.q: Why use the photo from above?
questions.a: Maps show land from above.

days.guide: Draw a map of your neighborhood or a park with natural features and a key.

questions.q: What natural features might you include?
questions.a: Hills, creeks, ponds, or the coast.

questions.q: Where does the key go?
questions.a: In a corner of the map.

days.guide: Compare the model and the map: what each shows well.

questions.q: What does the model show that the map doesn't?
questions.a: Height — how tall mountains are.

questions.q: What does the map show well?
questions.a: Shapes and where things are.

weeks.assessment_key: California map: Sierra Nevada (mountains along the east), Central Valley (middle), Sacramento River (flows south through the northern Central Valley toward San Francisco Bay), Lake Tahoe (on the eastern border with Nevada), Pacific coast (west). Map key with colors/symbols. Model map with key and compass rose. Comparison: map shows shapes and locations well; the model shows height (how tall mountains are).

weeks.prep: Gather a globe or world map, ice cubes, salt, and cups; find a short reading on the Sierra Nevada snowpack. Safety for the taste test: use clean drinking water and a pinch of table salt, tasting a tiny sip.
misconceptions: Thinking most of Earth's water is fresh. Most is salty ocean water; much of the fresh water is frozen.
Thinking water is only liquid. Water is also solid (ice, snow, glaciers).

days.guide: Spin a globe and stop it with a finger 20 times; tally land vs. water. Color oceans, ice caps, and large lakes.

questions.q: Did your finger land more on land or water?
questions.a: Water — most of Earth is covered by water (about 70%).

questions.q: What is the largest ocean?
questions.a: The Pacific Ocean.

days.guide: Observe ice melting; list where water is solid and where it is liquid on Earth.

questions.q: Name places where water is solid.
questions.a: Glaciers, ice caps, snow on mountains.

questions.q: Name places where water is liquid.
questions.a: Oceans, rivers, lakes.

days.guide: Read about the Sierra Nevada snowpack and draw water's path from snow to faucet.

questions.q: Where does the snowpack's water go in spring?
questions.a: It melts and flows into rivers and reservoirs.

questions.q: How does it reach your faucet?
questions.a: Through reservoirs, pipes, and water treatment to homes.

days.guide: Taste-test fresh and slightly salty water (tiny sip); sort water bodies into fresh and salt.

questions.q: Is ocean water fresh or salt?
questions.a: Salt.

questions.q: Is Lake Tahoe fresh or salt?
questions.a: Fresh.

days.guide: Give the unit quiz: label landforms and water on a map; identify solid and liquid water.

questions.q: Is a glacier solid or liquid water?
questions.a: Solid.

questions.q: Is a river solid or liquid?
questions.a: Liquid.

weeks.assessment_key: Water-sources chart: solid — glaciers, ice caps, snow (Sierra snowpack); liquid — oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds. Salt — oceans, bays; fresh — most lakes, rivers, ponds, snow, glaciers. Unit quiz: landforms and water correctly labeled on a map; solid vs. liquid places identified. Globe tally: usually about 7 of 10 stops land on water (Earth is about 70% water).

weeks.prep: Gather paper, 10 straws, craft sticks, 50 cm of tape, two stacks of books 20 cm apart, pennies, a paper cup with string, and the Unit 2 strength data.
misconceptions: Thinking a flat sheet of paper is strong. Folding paper (accordion) makes it much stronger.
Adding pennies unevenly or dropping them. Add one at a time gently.

days.guide: Define the problem: build a bridge across a 20-cm gap that holds a cup of pennies; list criteria and limits.

questions.q: What are the limits (constraints)?
questions.a: 10 straws, 1 sheet of paper, 50 cm of tape.

questions.q: What must the bridge do?
questions.a: Span 20 cm and hold a cup of pennies.

days.guide: Sketch two designs (flat, accordion, arch) and choose materials using strength data.

questions.q: Which shape is stronger: flat paper or accordion-folded paper?
questions.a: Accordion-folded.

questions.q: Why use earlier data?
questions.a: To choose the strongest materials.

days.guide: Build the bridge and check it spans the gap without touching the 'water.'

questions.q: How long must it be?
questions.a: Longer than 20 cm so it rests on both stacks.

questions.q: Why not touch the water?
questions.a: That's a rule of the challenge — the bridge must span the river.

days.guide: Hang a cup and add pennies one at a time; record when it sags or falls.

questions.q: How many pennies did it hold?
questions.a: Answer from data.

questions.q: Why add one at a time?
questions.a: To get an exact count.

days.guide: Change one part (fold the paper, add a straw truss) and retest.

questions.q: Did the change help?
questions.a: Answer from data.

questions.q: Why does folding help?
questions.a: Folds make the paper stiffer so it bends less.

weeks.assessment_key: Design sketches: two labeled designs (flat, accordion, or arch). Load-test data: pennies held before sagging/falling for the first and improved bridge (folded or trussed designs typically hold many more pennies than flat paper). Proficient: data recorded and the improvement explained ('folding the paper made it stiffer, so it held more pennies').

weeks.prep: Gather bridge data, the science notebook, a trifold or poster board, markers, and materials to demonstrate one investigation live. Prepare a year-end quiz (10 items).
misconceptions: Displays with pictures but no data. Each investigation needs question, test, data, and conclusion.
Mixing up reversible and irreversible on review. Ask 'Can it go back?'

days.guide: Make a T-chart comparing the first and improved bridges and explain which shape worked best.

questions.q: Which shape held more pennies?
questions.a: Answer from data (usually folded/accordion).

questions.q: Why?
questions.a: It was stiffer and spread the weight.

days.guide: Review the notebook and choose 3 favorite investigations to display.

questions.q: Why choose investigations with good data?
questions.a: Data shows what you found out.

questions.q: What was the question in the plant investigation?
questions.a: Do plants need light and water?

days.guide: Make a science fair board with question, test, data, and conclusion for each.

questions.q: What goes in the conclusion?
questions.a: What you found, with evidence.

questions.q: Why include a graph?
questions.a: It shows data clearly.

days.guide: Present the board and demonstrate one investigation live.

questions.q: What makes a strong presentation?
questions.a: Clear voice, showing data, explaining the conclusion.

questions.q: What will you demonstrate?
questions.a: Example: the absorbency test.

days.guide: Give the year-end review quiz.

questions.q: Is melting chocolate reversible?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: What do roots do to slow erosion?
questions.a: Hold soil in place.

weeks.assessment_key: Science fair rubric (3 = proficient): 3 investigations each with question, test, data, conclusion; one live demo explained clearly. Year-end quiz (suggested 10): 1) Best raincoat material — plastic (waterproof) 2) Melting ice — reversible 3) Cooking an egg — irreversible 4) Plants need light and water 5) Wind carries dandelion seeds 6) Bees move pollen 7) Desert animals survive with little water (e.g., tortoise in burrow) 8) Earthquake — fast change 9) Grand Canyon — slow change 10) Plant roots slow erosion.
